text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

DeCotiis v. DeCotiis Estate,

2023 BCSC 287

Date: 20230228

Docket:
S216393

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Ivano
DeCotiis

Plaintiff

And

The
Estate of Innocenzo DeCotiis Deceased by its executors, Rossano DeCotiis,
Giulio DeCotiis, IDC Alter Ego Trust (2019), Rossano DeCotiis and Giulio
DeCotiis in their capacity as Trustees of the IDC Alter Ego Trust (2019) and in
their personal capacity, Morris DeCotiis, Paolo DeCotiis, and RPMG Capital
Corp.

Defendants

Before: Master Bilawich

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

J.
Watson

Counsel for the Defendant Rossano De Cotiis:

A. Cocks

C. Bildfell

No other appearances.

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February
2, 2023

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February
28, 2023

Introduction

[
1
]

The defendant Rossano De Cotiis (“Rossano”) applies
to strike paras. 22–29 in part 1 of the amended notice of civil claim, on the
basis they are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous and vexatious; or that they
may prejudice, embarrass or delay a fair hearing or that they are an abuse of
process of the court.

[
2
]

The plaintiff Ivano De Cotiis (the “plaintiff”
or “Ivano”) opposes the application and says the impugned paragraphs are proper
and necessary.

[
3
]

It is my understanding there is a typographical
error in the parties’ surname as it appears in the style of cause and that the
proper spelling is “De Cotiis”. I will use the corrected form in these reasons.
Given that all of the parties have the same surname, so for the sake of clarity
I refer to them by their given names in these reasons. No disrespect is
intended to anyone involved.

Background

[
4
]

This litigation involves the estate of Innocenzo
De Cotiis (“Innocenzo” or the “Deceased”), who died on September 26, 2020 (the
“Date of Death”). He was a successful real estate developer who founded the
Onni group of companies (“Onni Group”). He is survived by seven children
including, from oldest to youngest: Donato, Vittorio, Ivano, Giulio, Rossano,
Morris and Paolo.

[
5
]

There is an unfortunate divide between the
siblings. I will refer to the three eldest (Donato, Vittorio, Ivano) as the
“Older Brothers” and the four youngest (Giulio, Rossano, Morris and Paolo) as
the “Younger Brothers”.

[
6
]

The plaintiff says that since the Date of Death,
neither he nor the other two Older Brothers have received any inheritance from
the Deceased’s estate, or anything from family trusts the Deceased established
while alive. He believes that the entirety of the estate and certain trust
assets have either passed to or are under the effective control of the Younger
Brothers, or some of them. The plaintiff seeks a variety of relief as against the
defendants.

Notice of Civil Claim

[
7
]

On July 12, 2021, the plaintiff filed the notice
of civil claim (“Original NCC”). Among his allegations, he says the Deceased
settled four trusts during his lifetime, including a 1987 Trust, 1988 Trust,
1993 Trust and 2019 Trust.

[
8
]

The 1987 and 1988 Trusts involved warehouse
properties in Coquitlam. These are described as “foundational properties” for what
eventually became the Onni Group. The plaintiff was initially a beneficiary of
both trusts.

[
9
]

The 1993 Trust held a variety of shares in a
company which eventually became Onni Development Corp., which is the central
corporate vehicle within the Onni Group. Shares in one or more other companies were
added later. The plaintiff says the purpose of this trust was to pass the “family
business” on to the Deceased’s seven children and their respective children (the
Deceased’s grandchildren).

[
10
]

The plaintiff alleges that in or about December 2014, the Deceased
purported to add himself as a beneficiary of the 1993 Trust, unlawfully
misappropriated the trust’s property and converted it to his own use, thereby depriving
the plaintiff of his share. Due to the Deceased’s breach of trust and fiduciary
duty, the plaintiff became a “creditor” of the Deceased as of those dates. This
plea is significant for purposes of relief the plaintiff claims under the
Fraudulent
Conveyance Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 163 (“
FCA
”).

[
11
]

The plaintiff says the 2019 Trust was created to hold various life
insurance policies which were taken out on the Deceased’s life. It is a
discretionary trust. The trustees are Rossano and Giulio. The beneficiaries initially
included the Deceased’s seven children. The plaintiff asserts that the 1993
Trust property was used to pay some or all of the premiums on these life insurance
policies. Following the Deceased’s death, roughly $34.8 million in insurance proceeds
were paid to the 2019 Trust.

[
12
]

The plaintiff alleges Rossano and Giulio, as trustees of the 2019 Trust,
loaned $34,190,000 in 2019 Trust property to RPMG Capital Corp. (“RPMG”), a
company owned or controlled by the Younger Brothers. By investing effectively the
entirety of the trust’s property into RPMG, Rossano and Giulio put the trust’s
property at risk and failed to exercise the level of care, skill, diligence and
judgment that a prudent investor would in making investments, as required by
the
Trustee Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 464 (“
TA
”), they acted in
conflict of interest and breached fiduciary duties owed to beneficiaries of the
2019 Trust, including the plaintiff.

[
13
]

The plaintiff also pled a will variation claim. He says the Deceased
had previously made several wills which named the plaintiff as a beneficiary.
On January 12, 2016, the Deceased made a new will (the “2016 Will”) which named
Rossano and Giulio as executors and trustees. It bequeaths the residue of the estate
to the Younger Brothers and disinherits the plaintiff and two other Older
Brothers.

[
14
]

In the “Relief Sought” section, the plaintiff claims damages for
breach of trust and fiduciary duty, tracing remedies in relation to 1987, 1988
and 1993 Trust property, tracing of other property the Deceased transferred
after the date on which the plaintiff became entitled to make a claim under the

FCA
, an order removing Rossano and Giulio as trustees of the 2019 Trust
and appointing an arm’s length qualified trust administrator, a declaration the
2016 Will fails to make adequate provision for the plaintiff pursuant to
s. 60

of the
Wills, Estates and Succession Act
, S.B.C. 2009, c. 13 (“
WESA
”)
and an order that adequate, just and equitable provision be made for the
plaintiff out of the Deceased’ estate.

[
15
]

In the “Legal Basis” section, the plaintiff includes sections
dealing with breaches of the 1987, 1988 and 1993 Trusts by the Deceased, constructive
or resulting trust due to misappropriation of the plaintiff’s share of the 1993
Trust, restitution, tracing, breach of the 2019 Trust by Rossano and Giulio, their
removal as trustees due to conflict of interest and self-dealing, variation of
the 2016 Will and fraudulent conveyance remedies.

Response to Civil Claim

[
16
]

On September 24, 2021, Rossano and Giulio filed a
response to civil claim (“RCC”). They admit the plaintiff was a beneficiary of
the 1987, 1988 and 1993 Trusts but say these trusts were fully discretionary. There
are numerous additional beneficiaries of the 2019 Trust and it was not created
solely to hold life insurance proceeds.

[
17
]

With respect to the 2016 Will, they admit
Rossano and Giulio are named as executors and trustees and that it bequeathed the
residue of the Deceased’s estate to the Younger Brothers. They say the 2016
Will does make just, adequate and equitable provision for the plaintiff because
he and the Deceased had been estranged since the mid-to-late 1990s. A key
allegation for purposes of this application is part 1, division 3, para. 20,
where it is alleged the plaintiff assaulted the deceased:

20. In or about
September 2004, the plaintiff physically assaulted the Deceased, resulting in
significant injuries which required medical attention, and caused the Deceased
to fear for his safety.

[
18
]

Rossano and Giulio say that a part of the 1987 Trust assets were distributed
to the plaintiff.

[
19
]

The 1988, 1993 and 2019 Trusts each included provisions stating that
the trustee’s exercise in good faith of the powers and discretion given to them
would not subject them to any liability of any kind. The 1988 and 1993 Trusts expressly
gave the trustee power to remove and exclude any person as a beneficiary, in
the trustee’s sole discretion. They say on or about June 19, 2008, the plaintiff
was removed and excluded as beneficiary of the 1988 and 1993 Trusts.

[
20
]

They allege the 2019 Trust gave the Deceased a power of appointment,
which he used on December 23, 2019 to execute a Deed of Appointment. That deed
directed the trustees to exclude a person as a Fund Beneficiary in the event he
commences any litigation against or in respect of the Trust, the Fund, the
Deceased’s estate or any company in which the Trust, the Deceased or his estate
has an interest. The plaintiff was excluded as a beneficiary of the 2019 Trust
on or about July 21, 2021, which I understand to refer to the date the
plaintiff filed his Original NCC in this matter.

[
21
]

Regarding the loan of 2019 Trust funds to RPMG, Rossano and Giulio
say the trustees are expressly permitted to enter into commercially reasonable
agreements with companies in which the trustees have an interest. They say the investment
with RPMG was prudent, involves a reasonable rate of return and is secured by personal
guarantees.

Amended Notice of Civil Claim

[
22
]

On October 26, 2022, the plaintiff filed an amended notice of civil
claim (“Amended NCC”). It purports to add Morris, Paolo and RPMG as defendants.
It does not appear this was done via a formal application to add defendants;
rather, it appears they were simply added through amendment. If the latter
approach was taken, the only avenue for adding a party to an action after it
has been started is pursuant to an application under Rule 6-2(7) of the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
(“
SCCR
”). See in this regard
Alexis v. Duncan
,

2015 BCCA 135
at para.
20

et seq
.

[
23
]

The plaintiff added allegations that he had been an integral member
of the Onni Group and corporate entities which preceded it. He performed a
number of jobs for the Deceased and various family companies, starting at age eight.
He worked continuously for the Deceased and the family businesses and gradually
took on larger roles with more responsibility. He left high school and began
working full-time. He served in several management roles, including Vice
President - Development and Project Manager. He says he was paid little or
nothing for his work but was assured at all times that he had an ownership
interest in them.

[
24
]

The amendments which are the focus of this
application to strike are part 1, paras. 22–29 (collectively, the “Impugned
Amendments”):

Childhood Trauma, Assault and Battery

22. For the purposes of this Amended Notice
of Civil Claim the three oldest sons of the Deceased: Donato Vittorio and Ivana
will be referred to as the "Older Brothers" and the four youngest
sons, Rossano, Guilio, Morris and Paolo, will be referred to as the
"Younger Brothers".

23. The Plaintiff and his brothers, and in
particular the Older Brothers, were the victims of abuse at the hands of their
father.

24. The Plaintiff was regularly assaulted and
battered by his father throughout his childhood and into his adulthood.

25. The Deceased also regularly assaulted
and battered the Plaintiff's mother Rosa, which was witnessed by [the
Plaintiff] and his brothers.

26. Violence between family members including
the Deceased was a regular occurrence and was directed at various family
members, including the mother of the Plaintiff and was perpetrated by the
Deceased and his brothers.

27. To the best of the Plaintiff's knowledge,
the Younger Brothers, or some of the[m] with the knowing approval of Rossano
and Guilio, retained people to physically assault the Plaintiff from various
times from approximately 2000 until 2006.

28. To the best
of the Plaintiff's knowledge, the Younger Brothers, or some of them with the
knowing approval of Rossano and Guilio, retained private investigators to
surveill the Plaintiff from approximately 2000 until 2020.

The Deceased's Desire for a United Family

29. Despite the
family's violence, and despite occasional disagreements and even physical
altercations between the Plaintiff and the Deceased, the Deceased remained at
all time[s] committed to providing for [the Plaintiff].

[
25
]

The plaintiff goes on to say that any temporary estrangement between
him and the Deceased was caused by the Younger Brothers. He alleges they threatened
to exclude the Deceased from their lives if he involved the plaintiff in
social, business or family affairs to a greater degree. He says the Deceased
expressed a constant and consistent desire for a united family and for each of
his seven children and their families (his grandchildren) to benefit equally
from the success of the family business.

[
26
]

The plaintiff added a section alleging the Younger Brothers unduly
influenced the Deceased and made decisions on his behalf. He says they harboured
a grudge against him which influenced their own decision making and the undue
influence they exerted upon the Deceased. The grudge arose because he made a
concerted effort to be part of their mother’s life after she and the Deceased were
divorced in 1993. The Younger Brothers sided with the Deceased and had little
or no interaction with their mother.

[
27
]

In the “Legal Basis” section, the plaintiff added paragraphs
addressing unjust enrichment and constructive trust based on work he did for
family businesses. He says he invested sweat equity which contributed to the
acquisition, preservation and maintenance of the tremendous wealth and success
of Onni Group, that the defendants were enriched thereby and there was no
juristic reason for the enrichment. The plaintiff made amendments addressing Rossano
and Giuilo’s alleged breaches of fiduciary duty in relation to the 2019 Trust, a
section regarding knowing receipt of trust property by Morris, Paolo and RPMG
and a section regarding undue influence and unconscionability invalidating unspecified
asset transfers and the 2016 Will.

[
28
]

For some of these newly added claims, there are no corresponding
amendments in the “Relief Sought” section. One example is the undue influence
claim relating to the 2016 Will. The plaintiff did not amend the “relief sought”
section to include a request that the 2016 Will be declared invalid. There is
also no clear relief sought relating to the new unjust enrichment and
constructive trust claims. These issues are not raised in this application, so I
will not comment further.

[
29
]

On December 23, 2022, Rossano’s counsel requested that the Impugned
Amendments be removed. Plaintiff’s counsel refused the request the same day.

Rossano’s Position

[
30
]

Rossano says the amended notice of civil claim
alleges six causes of action, including (a) breach of trust, (b) reach of
fiduciary duty, (c) knowing receipt of assets transferred in breach of trust
(d) fraudulent conveyance, (e) undue influence, (f) unconscionability (g) failure
to make adequate provision in the 2016 Will.

[
31
]

The plaintiff seeks a variety of relief
including (a) damages for breach of trust and breach of fiduciary duty, (b) tracing
of trust assets and property transferred after Ivano became entitled to make a
claim under the
FCA
, (c) removal of Rossano and Giulio as trustees of
the 2019 Trust, (d) a possible challenge to the validity of the 2016 Will and
unparticularized property transfers, and (e) will variation.

[
32
]

Counsel notes that despite adding a section entitled “Childhood
Trauma, Assault and Battery”, the plaintiff is not making any claims in tort.

[
33
]

Rossano says the Impugned Amendments do not help establish any of
the plaintiff’s causes of action. No attempt is made to link them to any particular
cause of action. If they do not advance a claim known in law, it is obvious
they cannot succeed or they serve no useful purpose and are a waste of the
court’s time and public resources. They distract from the real issues in the litigation
and draw the parties and the court into matters that are wholly apart from the
issues in dispute. Finally, he says they are an abuse of process, inflammatory
and “knowingly false”. They are included for the improper purpose of trying to
pressure, harass and embarrass the defendants.

Plaintiff’s Position

[
34
]

The plaintiff says the Impugned Amendments are relevant to several causes
of action.

[
35
]

Will Variation: These claims are fact-intensive. Family history and
relationships need to be reviewed. The family has a contentious history which necessitates
investigation of unpleasant and embarrassing matters, including childhood
assault by the Deceased. This is necessary for a fair trial. The defendants have
raised a September 2004 assault as an issue. This relates to estrangement and
disinheritance. It is necessary to put the incident into a broader context of
the history of family violence.

[
36
]

Fraudulent Conveyance: The plaintiff argues he had potential claims
in tort against the Deceased due to childhood assaults. This gives the
plaintiff standing as a “creditor or other” under s. 1 of the
FCA
and
allows him to challenge subsequent property transfers by the Deceased as void
as against him.

[
37
]

Unjust Enrichment / Constructive Trust: Counsel argues the childhood
assault issue is relevant to the constructive trust claim. If the plaintiff can
prove he was assaulted by the Deceased and witnessed assaults on other family
members, the court may be more inclined to grant him a constructive trust remedy.

[
38
]

Trustee Duties / Removal of Trustee: Counsel argues that allegations
the Younger Brothers hired private investigators to carry out surveillance of him
and arranged for others to assault him from time to time are relevant to
whether Rossano and Giulio, as trustees, have fulfilled fiduciary obligations owed
to beneficiaries and whether they should be removed. I presume this relates to the
2019 Trust.

[
39
]

Undue Influence: Counsel argues the foregoing surveillance and
assault allegations are also relevant to undue influence. If the Younger
Brothers are found to be responsible for those things, it is more likely they exerted
undue influence upon the Deceased to exclude the plaintiff.

Legal Basis

[
40
]

Rule 9-5(1) of the
SCCR
allows the court
to order the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document to be
struck out or amended on various grounds:

Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters

(1)

At any stage of a proceeding, the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition
or other document on the ground that

(a)
it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)
it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)
it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of
the proceeding, or

(d)
it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
41
]

Rossano relies upon sub-rules (b), (c) and (d).

Rule 9-5(1)(b) - Unnecessary, Scandalous, Frivolous or Vexatious

[
42
]

In
Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,
2020
SCC 5
at paras
65–66
:

[65]
Under rule 9-5(1)(b), a
pleading may be struck if "it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious". Fisher J. articulated the relevant considerations in
Willow v. Chong
,
2014
BCSC 1083
, stating:

Under Rule 9-5(1)(b), a pleading is
unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's
cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known in law, where it is
obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no useful
purpose and would be a waste of the court's time and public resources:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
[1999] BCJ
No. 2160
(SC (in chambers));
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA
629
. [at para. 20 (CanLII)]

[66]
This Court admonished
in
Imperial
Tobacco
that the motion to strike

is a tool that must be used with care. The law is not static and
unchanging. Actions that yesterday were deemed hopeless may tomorrow succeed...
. Therefore, on a motion to strike, it is not determinative that the law has
not yet recognized the particular claim. The court must rather ask whether,
assuming the facts pleaded are true, there is a reasonable prospect that the
claim will succeed. The approach must be generous and err on the side of
permitting a novel but arguable claim to proceed to trial. [para. 21]

[
43
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(S.C.) at para.
47
:

47
Irrelevancy and embarrassment
are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is difficult to
understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc.

(1987),

1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
,
17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.)
. An "embarrassing" and
"scandalous" pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it will
involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas
Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
,
62 B.C.L.R. 145
at 147 (B.C.C.A.)
. An
allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the
proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College
of Dental Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland

(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
,
66 W.W.R. 499
(B.C.C.A.)
. A pleading is
"unnecessary" or "vexatious" if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff's cause of action or does not advance any claim
known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.)

(B.C.S.C.)
. A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out if it is not
necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v. Canadian Puget
Sound Lumber and Timber Co.

(1920),
28 B.C.R. 39 (C.A.)
. A
pleading is "frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the
sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of
estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.
,
[1992] B.C.J. 1567
,
(6 July 1992), Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

Rule 9-5(1)(c) - May Prejudice, Embarrass or Delay the Fair
Trial or Hearing of the Proceeding

[
44
]

In
Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
,
[1985]
B.C.J. No. 2328
,
62 B.C.L.R. 145 (C.A.)
the court of appeal approved the
following definition of “embarrassing” pleadings:

7
In
Mahoney v. Coca
Cola Ltd.
, unreported, February 21, 1967, No. 1612/64, B.C.S.C., and
Maddison
v. Donald H. Bain Ltd.

(1928), 39 B.C.L.R. 460 (C.A.)
, the Courts
adopted this definition of "embarrassing" pleadings from
Mayor of
City of London v. Herner

(1914) 111 L.T. 512
at 514:

... ["embarrassing" means] that the allegations are so
irrelevant that to allow them to stand would involve useless expense, and would
also prejudice the trial of the action by involving the parties in a dispute
that is wholly apart from the issues. In order that allegations should be
struck out from a defence upon that ground ... their irrelevancy must be quite
clear and, so to speak, apparent at the first glance. It is not enough that on
considerable argument it may appear that they do not afford a defence.

[
45
]

In
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
[“
Sahyoun
”]
at para.
62
:

[62]
A
pleading can be embarrassing if it does not state the real issue in an
intelligible form. It can also be embarrassing if it is prolix, includes
irrelevant facts, argument or evidence. It can be prejudicial if it is designed
to or has the effect of confusing the defendant, making it difficult, if not
impossible, to answer;
Virk
at para. 75.

[
46
]

In
Gross v. Peak Products Manufacturing Inc.
,

2021 BCSC 2016
at para.
15
, Justice Tammen commented as follows regarding
prejudice or delay of a fair trial:

[15]
… In my view, the
offending portions also breach Rule 9-5(1)(c) in that they might prejudice or
delay a fair trial. At a minimum, those parts of the notice of civil claim
would exponentially expand the scope of document disclosure and likely oral
discovery. Such is not in keeping with the primary object of the
Supreme Court Rules
described
in Rule 1-3 as securing:

... the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every
pleading on its merits.

Rule 9-5(1)(d) - Otherwise an Abuse of the Process of the Court

[
47
]

Abuse of process is summarized in
First
Majestic Silver Corp. v. Santos
,
2012 BCCA 5
at para.
22
:

[22]
The doctrine of abuse of
process is a very broad and flexible mechanism to enable judges to prevent
abuses of the court's process. In
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
,
[2003]
3 S.C.R. 77
, at para.
35
, the Supreme Court of Canada adopted descriptions of
the concept of abuse of process as proceedings "unfair to the point that
they are contrary to the interest of justice" and "oppressive
treatment".

[
48
]

In
Sahyoun
at para.
60

[60]
The
abuse of process standard under R. 9-5(1)(d) derives from a flexible doctrine.
It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would
violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity
of the administration of justice;
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63
at
paras.
35-37
.

[
49
]

In
Canadian Federation of Students v. Simon
Fraser Student Society
,
2010 BCSC 1816
at paras.
40–41
, Justice Grauer, as
he then was, summarized as follows:

[40]
Rule 9-5(1)(c) and (d)
involve a number of considerations. These include whether the pleadings are
unintelligible, confusing and difficult to understand, whether they are so
irrelevant ("embarrassing" and "scandalous") that they will
involve the parties in useless expense and prejudice the trial by involving
them in a dispute that strays far from the issues, and whether they do not
advance any defence known to law ("unnecessary" or "vexatious").
See, for instance,
Moulton Contracting Ltd. v. British Columbia
,
2010
BCSC 506
, and the cases cited therein by Hinkson J., as he then was. These
considerations also encompass a pleading that is made for an improper purpose,
such as to harass and oppress the other parties, as opposed to raising a
bona fide
defence.

[41]
Rule
9-5(1)(d) also raises a number of considerations. A pleading is an "abuse
of the process of the court" not only if it attempts to re-litigate
something already decided, but also if it violates such principles as judicial
economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the administration of
justice: see, for instance,
Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang Holding Inc.
,
2009
BCSC 473
at para.
47
, citing
Toronto (City) v. Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2003]
3 S.C.R. 77 at para.
37
.

Analysis

Will Variation

[
50
]

The plaintiff argues the Impugned Amendments are
relevant to issues raised by his will variation claim.
Section 60
of
WESA

provides that if a will-maker dies leaving a will that does not, in the court's
opinion, make adequate provision for the proper maintenance and support of the
will-maker's spouse or children, it may order that the provision it thinks
adequate, just and equitable in the circumstances be made out of the
will-maker's estate.

[
51
]

Where, as here, the plaintiff has been
disinherited, the reasons for disinheritance are relevant. The defendants
appear to point to a longstanding estrangement and a September 2004 assault as
reasons for disinheritance under the 2016 Will. The plaintiff, through the
Impugned Amendments, seeks to put forward the broader context of his
relationship with the Deceased.

[
52
]

Authorities addressing will variation claims brought
by a child who was mistreated and disinherited by the will-maker are reviewed in

Persall v. Stromberg
,
2015 BCSC 1826
at paras.
77-85
. These
conclude that will variation is not intended to be an alternative means of awarding
compensation for abuse. However, historical mistreatment may still relevant. In

Doucette v. McInnes
,
2009 BCCA 393
at para.
71
, the court of appeal indicated
that a will-maker parent who treated their child unfairly may have a moral
obligation to make amends for that through their will:

[71]
It
is common ground that the
Wills Variation Act
is not intended as a
means of awarding compensation for family abuse, but as recognized
in
Sawchuk v.
MacKenzie Estate
,
2000 BCCA 10
, 72 B.C.L.R. (3d) 333 at
para.
16
, where a parent has treated a child unfairly, a judicious parent,
after objective reflection, would recognize a moral obligation to make amends
for it through the provisions of his or her will. In my view that is all that
the trial judge was doing in this case.

[
53
]

By alleging the plaintiff assaulted the Deceased in 2004, Rossano
and Giulio having have made family violence relevant to the matters in issue.
The plaintiff is entitled to respond to this, which he has chosen to do through
the Amended NCC rather than through a Reply. A broader history of family
violence between the plaintiff and the Deceased may be relevant to an assessment
of whether the Deceased’s disinheritance of the plaintiff was reasonable in the
circumstances. At this stage, I am not in a position to conclude that the
broader history of family violence between the plaintiff and the Deceased in
particular should be struck out.

[
54
]

However, I do not agree that the Impugned Amendments relating to historical
abuse the Deceased is alleged to have directed towards the plaintiff’s siblings
or his mother are relevant to will variation issues as between the plaintiff
and the Deceased.

Fraudulent Conveyance

[
55
]

The plaintiff argues that the childhood abuse he alleges means he
had potential claims in tort against the Deceased at times when the Deceased made
unparticularized property transfers. He argues this gave him standing as a
“creditor” of the Deceased under
s. 1
of the
FCA
. That section actually
refers to “creditors and others”. This should allow him to invoke the
FCA

to set aside any property transfers which occurred after he gained this status.

[
56
]

Plaintiff’s counsel did not refer me to any authorities where the
court has employed the
FCA
in a similar manner. I also note it is
arguably unnecessary for the plaintiff to invoke childhood assault to maintain
this argument, He is already advancing it by virtue of the Deceased’s alleged
breaches of the 1993 Trust. These allegations appear to have a more logical
connection to the property transfers the plaintiff seeks to challenge.

[
57
]

In my view, the historical abuse allegations are unnecessary,
prejudicial and embarrassing for purposes of the plaintiff’s fraudulent
conveyance claim.

Unjust Enrichment / Constructive Trust

[
58
]

The plaintiff argues that the claim in constructive trust is
impacted by the claims of historical abuse. Counsel argues that if the
plaintiff can prove he was assaulted and witnessed assaults on other family
members, the court may be more inclined to find a constructive trust in favour
of the plaintiff. Counsel refers to
BNSF Railway Company v. Teck Metals Ltd.
,

2016 BCCA 350
for the proposition that “good conscience” may require a finding
of constructive trust. He also suggests this may also involve a novel extension
of constructive trust law beyond the two types of situations where they are
typically found to exist – (a) where there has been a breach of fiduciary duty
or (b) unjust enrichment.

[
59
]

Counsel did not direct me to any authority which supports this
proposition. I conclude that the Impugned Amendments are unnecessary and irrelevant
to the plaintiff’s unjust enrichment / constructive trust claims.

Trustee’s Duties / Removal of Trustee

[
60
]

The plaintiff argues the Impugned Amendments which allege the
Younger Brothers hired private investigators to conduct surveillance on him
between 2000 and 2020 and retained people to physically assault him between
2000 and 2006 are relevant to whether Rossano and Giulio are meeting their
obligations as trustees of the 2019 Trust. They are also relevant to whether
they ought to be removed as trustees.

[
61
]

A summary of principles applicable to removal of
a trustee were summarized by Hinkson C.J.S.C. in
Parker v. Thompson
(Trustee)
,
2014 BCSC 1916
at paras.
35–40
. I will not reproduce the entire
excerpt here. Among the principles set out, the standard of conduct expected of
a trustee is set out at para. 36:

[36]
The
standard of conduct to be expected of a trustee in the administration of a
trust was not in dispute between the parties. It is as set out by Mr. Justice
Dickson, as he then was, for the Court at 315 in
Fales
v. Canada Permanent Trust Co.
,
1976 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, [1977] 2
S.C.R. 302:

Traditionally, the standard of care and diligence required of a
trustee in administering a trust is that of a man of ordinary prudence in
managing his own affairs (
Learoyd v.
Whiteley
[
(1887),
12 App. Cas. 727
.], at p. 733;
Underhill's Law of Trusts and Trustees
, 12th ed., art.
49;
Restatement of the Law on Trusts
, 2nd ed., para.
174) and traditionally the standard has applied equally to professional and
non-professional trustees. The standard has been of general application and
objective though, at times, rigorous. There has been discussion of the question
whether a corporation which holds itself out, expressly or impliedly, as
possessing greater competence and ability than the man of ordinary prudence
should not be held to a higher standard of conduct than the individual trustee.
It has been said by some that a higher standard of diligence and knowledge is
expected from paid trustees:
Underhill's Law
of Trusts and Trustees
, art. 49, relying upon
obiter
of Harman J.
in
Re Waterman's Will Trusts; Lloyds
Bank, Ltd. v. Sutton
[
[1952] 2 All E.R. 1054
.], at p. 1055, and upon
dicta
found in
National
Trustees Co. of Australasia v. General Finance Co. of Australasia
[
[1905] A.C.
373 (P.C.)
.], a case which did not turn upon the imposition of a greater
or lesser duty but upon the relief to which a corporate trustee might be
entitled under the counterpart of
s. 98
of the
Trustee
Act
of British Columbia, to which I have earlier referred.

[
62
]

The Chief Justice approved the following
principles for removal of a trustee, at para. 37:

(1)
the court will not lightly interfere with the testator's choice of
estate
trustee
;

(2)
clear evidence of necessity is required;

(3)
the court's main consideration is the welfare of the
beneficiaries; and

(4)
the estate
trustee
's acts or
omissions must be of such a nature as to endanger the administration of the
trust.

[
63
]

At paras. 39–40, the basis for removing trustees
and significance of past misconduct to the analysis is addressed:

[39]
It
is clear from the authorities that while actual dishonesty, lack of proper
capacity to execute his or her duties, or lack of reasonable fidelity are all
bases for
removing
a trustee
(
Re Commonwealth
Investors Syndicate Ltd.

(1986), 69
B.C.L.R. 346 at 356, [1986] B.C.J. No. 3112 (S.C.)
), even the
lesser basis of a
trustee
's
ability to act impartially may suffice to justify the removal of a
trustee
(
Re Shaw Co. Ltd.

(1922),
1922 CanLII 97 (SK KB)
,
68 D.L.R. 616
, [1922]
S.J. No. 89 (K.B)).

[40]
But
the removal of a
trustee

should not be lightly entertained. In
Radford
v. Radford Estate
(2008),
2008 CanLII 45548 (ON SC)
, 43 E.T.R.
(3d) 74, [2008] O.J. No. 3526, Mr. Justice Quinn discussed a number of
other considerations to apply when considering an application for the removal
of a trustee at paras. 102 -- 107:

Removal
must be the only course to follow

[102] Removal of an estate trustee should
only occur "on the clearest of evidence that there is no other course to
follow": see
Crawford v.
Jardine,

[1977] O.J. No. 5041 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
) at para. 18,
citing
Tempest, Re

(1866),
1 Ch.
App. 485 (Eng. C.A.)
and
Owen Family Trust,
Re

(1989),
33 E.T.R. 213
at 215 (B.C.S.C.)
.

Removal
to be guided by welfare of beneficiaries

[103] In deciding whether to remove an
estate trustee, "the court's main guide should be the welfare of the
beneficiaries": see
Crawford v.
Jardine, ibid
, citing
Letterstedt v.
Broers
(1884), (1883-84) L.R.
9 App. Cas. 371 (South Africa
P.C.)
at 385-387
and
Anderson, Re

(1928),
35
O.W.N. 7
at 8 (Ont. H.C.)
.

Non-removal
must likely prevent proper execution of trust

[104] "It is not every mistake or
neglect of duty on the part of the trustees which will lead to their
removal. It must be shown by the applicant that the non-removal of the trustee will
likely prevent the trust from being properly executed": see
Crawford v. Jardine, ibid.

[105] "[I]t is not indeed every mistake
or neglect of duty, or inaccuracy of conduct of trustees, which will
induce Courts of Equity to [remove trustees]. But the acts or omissions must be
such as to endanger the trust property or to shew a want of honesty or a want
of proper capacity to execute the duties, or a want of reasonable
fidelity": see
Letterstedt v.
Broers, ibid,
quoting s. 1289 of
Story's
Equity Jurisprudence
.

Removal
not intended to punish past misconduct

[106] "The authorities are, I believe,
consistent in placing the emphasis on the future administration of the estate,
and the risks to which it will be exposed if the trustee remains in office. The
question is whether the trust estate is likely to be administered properly in
accordance with the fiduciary duties of the trustee and with due regard to the
interests and welfare of the beneficiaries. The sanction of removal is intended
not to punish trustees for past misconduct but rather to protect the assets of
the trust and the interests of the beneficiaries": see
St. Joseph's Health Centre v. Dzwiekowski
,
supra
,
2007 CanLII 51347 (ON SC)
,
[2007] O.J. No. 4641
at para.
28
.

[107] But, "past misconduct that is likely to continue will
often be sufficient to justify removal ...": see
St. Joseph's Health Centre v. Dzwiekowski
,
supra
, at para. 29.

[
64
]

I am not persuaded that the allegations that Rossano and Giulio were
involved in or approved of other Younger Brothers arranging surveillance of and
assault upon the plaintiff are relevant to whether Rossano and Giulio
adequately carried out their duties as trustees of the 2019 Trust and were in
conflict of interest. These allegations are unnecessary, embarrassing and
prejudicial.

Undue Influence

[
65
]

The plaintiff argues that allegations that the Younger Brothers
hired private investigators to conduct surveillance on him between 2000 and
2020 and retained people to assault him from time to time between 2000 and 2006
are relevant to his claim in undue influence. If they are found to have done
these things, this makes it more likely that they exerted undue influence on
the Deceased to exclude the plaintiff.

[
66
]

I am not persuaded that the allegations that the Younger Brothers arranged
surveillance of and assaults upon the plaintiff are necessary to address
alleged undue influence of the Deceased. I am concerned that they would involve
an exponential expansion of the scope of discovery into irrelevant or at best
marginally relevant issues. These allegations are unnecessary, embarrassing and
prejudicial.

Conclusion

[
67
]

The application to strike paragraphs 22 and 24 of part 1 of the
Amended NCC are dismissed. For para. 24, further particulars of the alleged
assault and battery should be provided.

[
68
]

With respect to paragraph 29, the portions “Despite the family’s
violence,” is struck out and the balance of the paragraph shall remain.

[
69
]

The application to strike paragraphs 23, 25, 26, 27 and 28 are
granted.

[
70
]

Success has been divided on this application. Costs are in the
cause.
